title: IPAM exhaustion + kube-proxy fallback — incident notes and runbook sketch
content:
Status: draft notes for post-incident review and runbook sketch

Summary:
We observed a cluster-wide scheduling disruption caused by IP address exhaustion in the Calico IPAM pool combined with degraded kube-proxy dataplane behavior. Symptoms: pods in Pending state, frequent kubelet eviction churn on nodes that were actually under <50% memory, and a cascade of control-plane API timeouts as kube-proxy endpoints flapped. Impact window ~09:17–09:46 UTC on 2024-11-07.

High-level timeline (reconstructed):
- 09:12 UTC: autoscaling batch job (data-backfill) kicked off across ~1200 pods in a burst pattern.
- 09:16 UTC: spike in PodCreates observed (API server 429s briefly).
- 09:17 UTC: multiple nodes report "no available IPs" from calico-node logs; new pods fail with Pending + "failed to allocate address".
- 09:18 UTC: kube-proxy on several nodes starts reporting frequent conntrack errors and restarting; iptables rules churn noted.
- 09:20 UTC: scheduler queues backlog grows; some lower-priority pods are forced into Pending.
- 09:25 UTC: Kubelet eviction controller starts evicting pods on nodes with artificially inflated allocatable pressure (kubelet reported high ephemeral-port exhaustion and CNI plugin timeouts).
- 09:30 UTC: mitigation applied — scaled down the batch job by 75%, manually increased Calico IP pool size for cluster-internal pool on control plane (see commands below).
- 09:38 UTC: new pods slowly schedule as IPs are reclaimed and pool expanded; kube-proxy restarts stabilize.
- 09:46 UTC: control plane error budget returned to normal; incident declared resolved and narrowed to IPAM + kube-proxy interaction.

Initial hypothesis:
- The immediate root cause was IPAM pool exhaustion due to bursty pod creation without headroom in the per-node IP allocation policy.
- Secondary contributing factor: a bug in kube-proxy/version X.Y that mishandles rapid rule churn when endpoints are frequently created/removed, causing conntrack storms and transient packet drops which led kubelet to report network failures and trigger evictions.

Evidence & logs (snippets):
- calico-node log (node-ip-12):
  "ERROR ipam: no available IPs in pool default-pool for host 10.128.12.85"
- kube-proxy (node-ip-34):
  "E1123 09:18:42.123 kube-proxy.go:345] Failed to sync iptables: conntrack: unable to create entry"
- kubelet eviction message (node-ip-34):
  "evicting pod because node had unreachable for 30s; reason: NetworkUnavailable"
- kube-apiserver metrics: pod_creates/s spike to 1500/s for 60s at 09:16–09:17

Quick mitigations applied during incident:
- throttled the backfill job via CI pipeline -> scaled down replicas from 1200 to 300. (manual rollback flagged in SRE-4123)
- increased Calico IPv4 pool CIDR by adding a secondary pool and enabling auto-assign for that pool:
  calicoctl apply -f - <<EOF
  apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
  kind: IPPool
  metadata:
    name: extra-pool-2
  spec:
    cidr: 10.140.0.0/16
    ipipMode: Never
    natOutgoing: true
  EOF
- restarted kube-proxy on the subset of nodes showing conntrack errors for faster recovery: kubectl rollout restart daemonset/kube-proxy -n kube-system --selector=node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=

What worked:
- Rapid identification of IPAM error strings in calico logs led to correct immediate action (pool expansion).
- Scaling back the producer workload reduced new allocations and allowed pool reclamation.
- Rolling restart of kube-proxy on affected nodes reduced conntrack churn.

What didn't work / surprises:
- Auto-scaling job had no graceful ramp configured; should have been rate-limited by orchestration.
- Kubelet eviction decision relied on transient network failures rather than sustained resource exhaustion — policy may be too aggressive for transient CNI timeouts.
- Some IPs were stuck in "reserved" state due to intermittent calico-node failures and were not reclaimed quickly. Need to check reclaim loops.

Runbook sketch (for on-call use):
1) If pod creation failures with "no available IPs":
   - Check calico-node logs: kubectl logs ds/calico-node -n kube-system --tail=200 | grep "no available IPs"
   - Check pool utilization: calicoctl get ippools -o wide
   - If pool < 10% headroom, create secondary pool OR expand primary pool (see templates below).
2) To reduce immediate pressure:
   - Identify and throttle the largest pending/producer workloads (CI jobs, backfills). Use kubectl scale or pause pipeline.
3) If kube-proxy conntrack errors present:
   - Check kube-proxy logs and conntrack count: ssh to node -> conntrack -S and sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max
   - Consider kubectl rollout restart daemonset/kube-proxy -n kube-system for subset first.
4) Evictions triggered due to transient network failures:
   - Avoid cordoning nodes unless node shows persistent kernel-level failures.
   - Where possible, set eviction thresholds to prefer pod termination over eviction for network transient issues. Task: review eviction configuration defaults (kubelet eviction-hard/soft).
5) Post-incident: run reclaim script to sweep stale IP allocations (see linked PR).

Commands / helper snippets:
- calico pool list: calicoctl get ippools -o wide
- create pool (template): same as above in mitigation
- scan for reserved IPs: calicoctl get ipamblocks -o yaml | grep -B3 reserved
- conntrack summary: sudo conntrack -S | head -n 40

Action items (owners):
- SRE: implement IPAM headroom alerting on pool utilization > 75% (Aisha) — SRE-4124
- Infra: add rate-limiting gate for high-concurrency batch jobs (Tom) — PR in infra repo
- Platform: test kube-proxy X.Y+1 against synthetic churn workload and rollback if unstable (Ravi) — schedule 2024-11-15
- Calico/Networking: add reclaim job that forcibly frees IPs in "reserved" state older than 10m (Elena) — prototype PR #278

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Why did calico-node mark IPs reserved and not quickly reclaim after pod deletion? Is there a known bug with our calico version?
- Does kube-proxy have a known regression for rapid endpoint churn (tracked by upstream)?
- Consider changing default pod density per node or switch to a CNI mode with denser addressing (e.g., host-local with secondary pools). Tradeoffs required.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Add a guard in CI that prevents more than N concurrent job replicas across cluster (global concurrency limiter).
- Add CNI chaos-testing in chaos-runner to reproduce churn and ensure kube-proxy stability.
- Consider moving heavy burst workloads to separate node pools with dedicated IP pools to limit blast radius.

References & artifacts:
- Incident ticket: SRE-4123
- Calico reclaim PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/278
- Design notes: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/CNI+IPAM+Design

Draft status: needs follow-up on PRs and test schedule; will convert to formal postmortem once root cause confirmed and actions implemented.

-- Aisha (on-call)
